42860146.label: Background
42860146.text: Subclinical leaflet thrombosis is common after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) and may contribute to structural valve deterioration over time, this may be influenced by transcatheter heart valve (THV) design and other valve-related factors.

42860146.label: Methods
42860146.text: The "Effect of Subclinical Leaflet Thrombosis and Prosthesis Type on Transcatheter Aortic Valve Degeneration (POPular PET TAVI)" study is an international, multicenter, and cross-sectional cohort study. Patients (N = 180) are enrolled at five years after TAVI for a detailed assessment of THV structure and function using a multimodality imaging approach. High-resolution four-dimensional cardiac computed tomography (4D-CT) is used to assess subclinical leaflet thrombosis and THV characteristics (eg, neosinus volume, prosthesis deformation index, valve expansion, and commissural alignment). 18F-sodium fluoride (18F-NaF) positron emission tomography (PET) is used to measure microcalcification activity in the THV leaflets as a marker of structural valve deterioration. Transthoracic echocardiography is performed to evaluate THV and cardiac function. Obtained images are analyzed by dedicated core laboratories for PET and 4D-CT. To facilitate comparisons between balloon-expandable, intra-annular and self-expanding, supra-annular prostheses, enrollment is stratified for valve size and type. As of September 2026, 159 patients have been enrolled successfully, and completion is anticipated in May 2027.

42860146.label: Conclusions
42860146.text: The POPular PET TAVI study evaluates the interplay between subclinical leaflet thrombosis, THV characteristics, and structural valve deterioration at five years after TAVI. Improved understanding of these mechanisms may inform individualized antithrombotic strategies and optimized valve design, aiming to enhance long-term valve durability.

42861496.label: Background
42861496.text: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring is a useful tool for coronary heart disease (CHD) risk prediction. The current standard method, the Agatston score, weights plaque area upward by density. However, higher density is inversely associated with CHD. We aimed to develop and validate a CAC score accounting for the inverse association of density with CHD, and the nonlinear association between CAC volume and density in a prospective cohort study.

42861496.label: Methods
42861496.text: A CAC volume and density score was developed, which adjusts CAC volume for density based on whether the volume level was <130 mm3. We used data from the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) to develop and assess the score, including all participants with CAC>0 and follow-up for CHD events. Score performance for CHD risk prediction was compared with the pooled cohort equations and the Agatston score using Cox proportional hazards models and Harrell C-index and continuous and categorical net reclassification improvement. Analyses were also stratified by Agatston score, age, sex, race/ethnicity, and statin use. Finally, performance was evaluated in 4 longitudinal cohorts for external validation.

42861496.label: Results
42861496.text: The MESA cohort included 3360 individuals. CAC volume and density score improved the C-index for CHD to a greater degree over the pooled cohort equation (0.699 [95% CI, 0.675-0.723]) compared with the Agatston score (0.687 [95% CI, 0.663-0.711]) and resulted in greater continuous net reclassification improvement (0.54 [95% CI, 0.43-0.64]) compared with the Agatston score (0.45 [95% CI, 0.34-0.56]) when added to the pooled cohort equation. The greatest improvement in risk prediction was in those with lower burden of CAC (Agatston <300). Consistent results were seen in stratified analyses and external validation cohorts.

42861496.label: Conclusions
42861496.text: The CAC volume and density score, which adjusts CAC volume downward for higher density, and can be calculated from existing CAC reports, significantly improves risk discrimination and reclassification compared with the Agatston score.

42879296.text: The ureter is an important conduit between the kidney and the bladder and is frequently imaged to rule out cancer in the upper genitourinary tract. However, while malignancy can occur, a spectrum of other pathologic ureteral findings can exist, and these can be divided into congenital, intrinsic, and extrinsic abnormalities that range from postoperative and neoplastic conditions to inflammatory disease. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the ureter, including the ureteral anatomy, ureteral imaging strategies, and various ureteral conditions and their associated imaging features. It is important to identify congenital genitourinary variants, as these are frequently linked to further imaging recommendations, such as nuclear medicine renography and fluoroscopic voiding cystourethrography. Intrinsic abnormalities can be iatrogenic, infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic. Intrinsic ureteral strictures are most commonly iatrogenic, usually resulting from prior surgery or radiation therapy. Ureteral infections include tuberculosis, schistosomiasis, and Escherichia coli infection, which have varying imaging manifestations. Inflammatory conditions include ureteritis cystica and pseudodiverticulosis. Ureteral masses are rarely benign and are most commonly urothelial carcinomas. Processes in the abdomen and pelvis, including mass effect from pregnancy, ureteral compression from advanced pelvic floor prolapse, and rarely, ureteral obstruction from vaginal devices, also can affect the ureter. The ureter can be injured during pelvic surgery or trauma. It also may be involved by deep pelvic endometriosis, mass effect from extrinsic lesions, or reactive change from inflammatory processes. Radiologists need to have a clear understanding of the patient's history and the range of possible ureteral conditions to establish the optimal differential diagnosis.

42955096.label: Purpose
42955096.text: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the diagnostic performance of FDG PET/MR for detecting hepatic metastases from extrahepatic primary malignancies, together with acquisition protocols, reconstruction parameters, and technical heterogeneity.

42955096.label: Methods
42955096.text: A systematic search was conducted through September 2026. Eligible studies evaluated FDG PET/MR for hepatic metastases and reported diagnostic performance data and/or technical protocol information. Summary estimates of sensitivity and specificity were obtained using a bivariate random-effects model. A structured qualitative assessment of PET and MR acquisition, reconstruction parameters, and image interpretation strategies was also performed.

42955096.label: Results
42955096.text: Fifteen studies involving 861 patients met the inclusion criteria. Eight studies (53%) provided sufficient data for the diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis, whereas all contributed to the qualitative technical assessment. The meta-analysis demonstrated a summary sensitivity estimate of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.89-0.97) and a summary specificity estimate of 0.99 (95% CI, 0.92-1.00) for detecting hepatic metastases. Sensitivity showed substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 0.83), whereas specificity showed low heterogeneity (I² = 0.21). Technical assessment revealed marked variability in PET acquisition, MR protocols, reconstruction parameters, and reporting, with frequent underreporting of voxel size, filtering, and motion correction. Hepatobiliary contrast agents were used in only a minority of studies, and dedicated PET motion correction was rarely implemented.

42955096.label: Conclusion
42955096.text: FDG PET/MR demonstrates high lesion-level diagnostic accuracy for the detection of hepatic metastases, with high summary sensitivity and specificity. However, substantial between-study variability in sensitivity, together with variability and frequent underreporting of technical parameters, highlights the need for standardized acquisition protocols and reporting frameworks to improve reproducibility, comparability, and clinical translation.

42978146.label: Background and aims
42978146.text: The long-term prognostic value of a guideline-recommended selective sequential anatomical-functional imaging strategy using coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) followed by quantitative [15O]H2O positron emission tomography (PET) remains uncertain. We evaluated its long-term prognostic value in patients with first symptoms suggestive of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD).

42978146.label: Methods
42978146.text: In this multicentre European cohort, symptomatic patients first underwent CCTA and were selectively referred to quantitative [15O]H2O PET in case of suspected obstructive stenosis (≥50%). Patients were stratified according to CCTA findings and PET-derived ischaemia (normal CCTA; non-obstructive CAD on CCTA; obstructive CAD on CCTA without ischaemia; obstructive CAD on CCTA with ischaemia). The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), and hospitalization for unstable angina (UA). Adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) were calculated.

42978146.label: Results
42978146.text: Among 3,918 patients (61.0±9.8 years; 54.3% female) with a median follow-up of 5.1 [3.8-8.0] years, 278 (7.1%) experienced the primary endpoint. aHRs increased stepwise across CCTA-PET categories. Compared to normal CCTA, non-obstructive CAD and obstructive CAD without ischaemia were associated with a higher risk of the combined primary endpoint (aHR 1.89, [95%CI: 1.23-2.91], p=0.004; aHR 3.20, [95%CI: 1.95-5.25], p<0.001). Among patients with obstructive CAD on CCTA, PET-derived ischaemia further increased the risk of the primary endpoint (aHR 1.55, [95%CI: 1.05-2.30]; p=0.029), but not when excluding UA from the composite endpoint (aHR 1.37, [95%CI 0.90-2.07]; p=0.141). PET-derived ischaemia primarily predicted events within the first year, while obstructive CCTA findings remained associated with long-term hard outcomes.

42978146.label: Conclusions
42978146.text: A sequential strategy combining CCTA and quantitative [15O]H2O PET provides robust and incremental long-term risk stratification. While PET-derived ischaemia refines prediction of short-term and symptom-driven events, CCTA-derived CAD remains the principal determinant of long-term hard outcomes.

42998146.label: Objectives
42998146.text: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of ultrasound-derived fat fraction (UDFF) and auto-point shear wave elastography (Auto-pSWE) in bariatric surgery candidates, identify biological variables independently associated with their values and monitor postoperative changes in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) patients.

42998146.label: Methods
42998146.text: This prospective study enrolled patients who underwent UDFF and Auto-pSWE examinations within 3 days before bariatric surgery (October 2023-February 2025), with intraoperative biopsy as reference. Diagnostic performance of UDFF and Auto-pSWE (which measured shear wave velocity, SWV) were analyzed by receiver operating characteristic analysis. Multivariable generalized linear models identified variables independently associated with UDFF and SWV. Postoperative follow-ups were conducted at 3 and 6 months in MASLD patients.

42998146.label: Results
42998146.text: A total of 237 patients (mean age, 29.42 ± 9.37; 98 men) were included. UDFF showed excellent diagnostic performance for steatosis grades (AUCs: 0.991 for ≥S1, 0.911 for ≥S2, and 0.831 for ≥S3), with steatosis percentage as the strongest independent correlate (partial R2=0.302). SWV exhibited moderate diagnostic performance for significant fibrosis (AUC = 0.752), with fibrosis stages and alanine aminotransferase showing similar independent explanatory power (partial R2=0.067 and 0.063, respectively). In 104 MASLD patients, median UDFF decreased substantially by approximately 80% at 6 months while SWV transiently rose at 3 months before returning to a level comparable to baseline at 6 months.

42998146.label: Conclusion
42998146.text: UDFF provides accurate assessment of steatosis and shows potential for postoperative monitoring, whereas Auto-pSWE demonstrates moderate performance for significant fibrosis and transient postoperative changes, supporting its complementary rather than standalone role.

43020696.text: Enfortumab vedotin (EV), an anti-nectin-4 antibody-drug conjugate, alone and with pembrolizumab (EV plus pembrolizumab [EV/P]), has transformed the treatment of locally advanced/metastatic urothelial carcinoma (la/mUC), yet remains biomarker agnostic. We prospectively evaluated [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-N188 PET/CT ([68Ga]-N188 PET/CT) as a whole-body alternative for nectin-4 imaging, with [18F]-FDG PET/CT as an active comparator and conventional computed tomography as the reference standard for staging la/mUC in 25 patients planned for EV/P. [18F]-FDG PET/CT showed a higher maximum standardized uptake value and tumor-to-background ratio than [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT across most lesion types (primary tumor, visceral, and osseous), except for lymph nodes. The overall tracer correlation was weak (Spearman r = 0.196), strongest in lymph nodes (r = 0.657), and absent in primary tumors and bone lesions. For primary tumor detection, [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT had higher specificity (86% vs 57%) and positive predictive value (92% vs 83%) than FDG, which had higher sensitivity (88% vs 67%). Nodal staging performance was similar in the tracers. For distant metastases, both achieved 100% sensitivity and negative predictive value, with [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT showing marginally higher specificity. [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT is feasible for whole-body nectin-4 assessment in la/mUC and supports a distinct biodistribution from FDG, suggesting complementary rather than interchangeable roles. Further prospective evaluation with treatment-outcome correlation is warranted before its use as a biomarker to guide EV-based therapy selection.
